header: IIT THE PESHAtrIAR HIGH COURT, BANIITU BENCH, BANITU
For the appealer(s) M/s Muhammad and Farid Ullah Shah
For the respondent(s) Mr. Ashiq Hussain, Advocate.
body: AURANGZEB J.- Through the instant Criminal Appeal, the complainant, Wakil Khan, has challenged the order dated 13.01.2026, passed by the learned Additional Sessions JudgeJI, Lakki Marwat, in Criminal Complaint No. 4/Comp of 2025, whereby his complaint under Sections 3 and 4 of the Illegal Dispossession Act, 2005 (hereinafter referred to as "the Act") was dismissed as not maintainable. The appellant seeks setting aside of the impugned order and remand of the complaint to the leamed trial court for recording of evidence and its decision on merits.

2. The case of the complainant, in brief, is that he is the owner of a house measuring four kanals, situated in Khata No. 1242, Khasra No. 3134, Moza Tattar Khel, Tehsil Ghazni Khel, District Lakki Marwat. He alleged that, on 01 .05.2025, at about 9:00 a.m., the respondents forcibly entered the house and dispossessed him. According to him, the respondents have no lawful connection with the property and are neither co-sharers nor owners thereof through any registered deed or mutation. As his efforts to resolve the matter amicably proved unsuccessful, he instituted the complaint on 15.05.2025, whereupon his statement was recorded under Section 20O, Cr.P.C.

3. After recording the complainant's statement, the learned trial court directed the concerned SHO to inquire into the matter. Pursuant thereto, the Patwari Halqa, accompanied by the police, inspected the site in the presence of both parties, measured the land and prepared a site plan. According to his report, based on the periodical record for 2013-L4, Khasra No. 3134, measuring twelve kanals and recorded in Khata No. 1242, was jointly owned, with the complainant being one of its owners, whereas the respondents were not recorded as owners. Respondent No. 2, Abdur Rahim, claimed before the police that he had constructed a house on the land in 2015 and undertook to produce documentary proof of its purchase from the complainant.

4. Upon receipt of the inquiry report, the learned trial court summoned the respondents, who appeared and contested the complaint. After hearing arguments on the question of maintainability, the learned trial court considered a receipt dated 09.08.2015, along with copies of the plaint and written statement relating to a civil suit instituted by the complainant and others against the respondents, pending before tJle learned Civil Judge-II, Lakki Marwat, and fixed for 31.01.2026. Without framing a charge or recording evidence, the learned trial court held that the civil court had already taken cognizance of the matter, that the dispute was prima facie civil in nature and that forcible dispossession could not be inferred from the police report. Consequently, the complaint was dismissed as not maintainable vide order dated 13.01.2026. Hence, the instant appeal.
5. I have heard the learned counsel for the parties and have gone through the record with their able assistance.

6. Before examining the controversy, it would be appropriate to consider the object and scope of the Act and the statutory provisions governing proceedings for illegal dispossession. The preamble of the Act reads as follows:

"WHEREAS it is expedient to protect the lawful owners and occupiers of immovable properties from their illegal or forcible dispossession therefrom by the property grabbers." The preamble reflects tJle legislative intention to protect lawful owners and occupiers of immovable property against illegal or forcible dispossession and to provide an effective remedy against such acts. The Act is a special enactment intended to prevent persons from taking the law into their own hands and unlawfully dispossessing those entitled to possess immovable property. Its object cannot, however, be understood to mean that every dispute relating to immovable property necessarily attracts criminal liability. The applicability of the Act depends upon the ingredients of the offence prescribed by its substantive provisions.

7. Section 2(c) ofthe Act defines an "occupier2 as uthe person who is in lawful possession of a propert5/, whereas Section 2(d) defines an "owne/ as the person who actually owns the property at the time of his dispossession, otherwise than through a process of law. Section 2(e) defines "properQ/ as immovable property' The distinction between an owner and an occupier is material because the protection afforded by the Act is not confined to ownership alone; a person in lawful possession is also entitled to its protection. The Act does not separately define the expressions "complainant' or "complaint". These expressions must, therefore, be understood in the context of the statutory scheme and the applicable criminal procedure. A complaint under the Act invokes the jurisdiction of the court of session to examine an allegation of illegal dispossession, while tJre person instituting it must establish, through legally admissible material, the facts necessary to attract the relevant penal provision.
8. Section 3(l) of the Act Provides:

"No one shall enter into or upon any property to dispossess, grab, control or occupy it without having any lawful authority to do so with tJle intention to dispossess, grab, control or occupy the property from owners or occupier of such propertSr.' Section 3(2) prescribes punishment for contravention of subsection (1), including imprisonment which may extend to ten years and line, in addition to compensation to the victim in accordance with Section 544- A of the Code of Criminal Procedure, 1898. Section 3(3), inserted through the Itlegal Dispossession (Amendment) Act, 2017, separately addresses the case of a person who forcibly and wrongfully dispossesses an owner or occupier of property where the act does not fall within subsection (1), and provides punishment which may extend to three years, or fine, or both, besides compensation in accordance with Section 544-A of the Code.

9. The language of Section 3 is significant. The expressions "no one" and "whoever" are general and comprehensive and do not restrict the operation of the Act to persons having the antecedents of professional land grabbers or members of a so-called Qabza Group. The essential inquiry is whether the conduct alleged falls within the statutory provision invoked and whether the accused committed the prohibited act without lawful authority. At the same time, the mere existence of a dispute over immovable property, or a disagreement concerning its title or possession, does not by itself establish an offence. The relevant ingredients must be examined in the light of the pleadings and evidence' 10. The scope of the Act was authoritatively considered by the Hon'ble Supreme Court in @ttlsho;n Blbl v. Muhammad. Sadlq (PLD 2076 SC 7691. and the principle was reiterated in Slulkh Muha nnad Noseem o. Fortda eul l20l 5 SCrtR I93 7t. The Hon'ble Supreme Court held that the use of the expressions "no one" and "whoever" in Section 3 does not confine prosecution to a particular category of offenders. The reference to "property grabbers" in the preamble cannot be employed to curtail the otherwise clear and unambigu'ous language of the substantive provision. The court is required to determine whether the offence described in the complaint has taken place and whether the accused committed it without lawful authority, rather than insisting upon proof that the accused has a prior history of land grabbing' ll.Thepreambleisanaidtounderstandingtheobjectoflegislation; it cannot override or restrict clear statutory language. Accordingly, the Act protects lawful owners and occupiers against illegal dispossession irrespective of whether the alleged offender is a professional land grabber. The prosecution must nevertheless establish the ingredients of the particular offence charged, and the Act cannot be used merely as a substitute for civil proceedings for determination of title ' 12. Section 4 of the Act provides the statutory basis for cognizance of the offence. Under subsection (1), notwithstanding anything contained in the Code or any other law for the time being in force, contravention of Section 3 is triable by the Court of Session on a complaint. Subsection (2) declares the offence under the Act to be non-cognizable, while subsection (3) empowers the Court, at any stage of the proceedings, to direct the police to arrest the accused. The significance of Section 4 is that the legislature has expressly conferred jurisdiction upon the Court of Session to adjudicate complaints alleging illegal dispossession. The proceedings are required to be conducted in accordance with the special procedure prescribed by the Act, read with the applicable provisions of the Code of Criminal Procedure, 1898, insofar as they are not inconsistent with the special enactment. The question whether the complaint ultimately succeeds is distinct from the question whether it is maintainable. At the threshold, the Court must examine whether the allegations, if established, disclose an offence under the Act. Where disputed questions of possession, authorit5r to occupy or the genuineness of a claimed transaction require evidence, such questions ordinarily cannot be conclusively determined merely by hearing arguments on maintainability.

13. Section 5 of the Act prescribes the procedure for investigation and trial. Under subsection (1), upon receipt of a complaint, the Court may direct the officer in charge of a police station to investigate the matter and submit a report within fifteen days, subject to extension where good reasons are shown. The proviso inserted through the 2Ql7 amendment further empowers the Court, where a local inquiry is necessary, to direct a Magistrate or revenue officer of the district to conduct the inquiry and submit a report within the period specified by the Court. Such a report is expressly to be construed as evidence in the case.

14. Subsection (2) requires the Court, upon taking cognizance, to proceed with the trial from day to day and decide the case within sixty days, recording sufficient reasons for any delay. Subsection (3) prohibits adjournment except where necessary in the interest of justice and provides that no adjournment shall, in any case, be granted for more than seven days. Subsection (4), introduced by the 2Ol7 amendment, empowers the Court, upon conclusion of the trial' to award compensatory costs up to five hundred thousand rupees where the complaint is found to be false, frivolous or vexatious.

15. These provisions demonstrate that the legislature intended proceedings under the Act to be expeditious while preserving a fair opportunity for the parties to establish their respective cases. The prescribed procedure does not authorize the Court to determine disputed facts on the basis of unproved documents or to dismiss a complaint merely because the parties are also litigating before a civil court. Equally, the special procedure does not dispense with the requirement of a fair trial or the need to establish the ingredients of the alleged offence.
16. The effect of tJle pendency of civil litigation upon proceedings Mst.

under the Act was considered in Shalkh Mu Iilaseem @ttl l2O16 SCMR I 9311. wherein, relying upon Grtlshan Blbl a. Muhammad Sadlq PLD 2O16 sc 7691. the Hon'ble Supreme Court hetd that the pendency of a civil suit concerning the same property does not, by itself, bar proceedings under the Act. Where the same transaction gives rise to civil liability as well as criminal consequences, the respective proceedings may operate independently in accordance with law. A person cannot take the law into his own hands and then seek to defeat criminal proceedings merely by pointing to the pendency of a civil suit. The aforesaid principle was reaffirmed by the Hon'ble Supreme Court in Oatsar Jabbar a. Sued. u Slrr,h and others 0PLD 2026 SC 3331. It was held that the jurisdiction of the Sessions court under the Act is not intended to determine complex questions of civil title; rather, the Court is required to examine the available material to ascertain whether a case of illegal dispossession is made out. A complaint cannot be summarily dismissed solely because a civil dispute concerning the property is pending, unless the Court, on a proper assessment of the circumstances, concludes that the proceedings amount to an abuse of the process of law or an attempt to convert a purely civil dispute into criminal proceedings' Even where the parties are co-owners of unpartitioned property, the relationship of coownership does not, by itself, dispense witl. the need to examine the allegation of dispossession in accordance with law' 17. Examined in the light of the foregoing statutory provisions and principles, the impugned order cannot be sustained. The learned trial court dismissed the complaint primarily on the ground that a civil suit concerning the property was pending between the parties. The pendency of such litigation, by itself, does not constitute a lawful ground for dismissal under the Act. No frnding was recorded that the complaint amounted to an abuse of the process of law or was intended to convert a purely civil dispute into criminal proceedings. Nor was the complaint examined through the process of evidence to determine whether the allegations disclosed an offence under Section 3.

18. In the present case, the complainant asserts ownership of the property and alleges that the respondents forcibly entered it and dispossessed him on 01.05.2025. The revenue record and the Patwari's report indicate that Khasra No. 3134, measuring twelve kanals and recorded in Khata No. L242, was jointly owned, with the complainant being one of its owners, whereas the respondents were not recorded as owners. Respondent No. 2, on the other hand, claimed that he had constructed a house on the land in 2015 and undertook to produce documentary proof of its purchase from the complainant' Lg. The police inquiry report, as obtained in the present proceedings, was prepared pursuant to a direction to the concerned sHo to inquire into the matter. Although the report and the revenue record constitute relevant material for consideration, they do not, in the circumstances of this case, conclusively determine the disputed questions of possession and the alleged transaction. The statutory proviso to Section 5(1), which expressly treats a report of a Magistrate or revenue officer as evidence' applies where the court directs such an officer to conduct a local inquiry underthatprovision.Therecordpresentlydescribedindicatesan inquiryinitiatedthroughtheSHo,duringwhichthePatwariinspected thesiteintJrepresenceoft}reparties.Thelegaleffectandevidentiary value of the material must, therefore, be assessed in accordance with the applicable statutory procedure and the nature of the inquiry actually conducted.

20. The receipt dated O9.08.2O15, relied upon by the respondents at the stage of arguments, has not been proved or tested through evidence' Whether the complainant was in possession of the property on 01.05.2025, whether the respondents unlawfully entered the property, whether the alleged transaction of sale is genuine and whether the respondents possessed any lawful authority to occupy the disputed property are questions of fact requiring determination after the parties have been afforded an opportunit5r to produce evidence. The claim of ownership, the nature of possession and the alleged sale transaction must be assessed in accordance urith 1aw, without treating the revenue record as conclusive proof of every disputed fact or accepting an unproved receipt as an established transaction.

21. The learned trial court, therefore, could not lawfully resolve these disputed questions at the threshold merely on the basis of the documents produced during arguments. Its conclusion that forcible dispossession could not be inferred, without recording evidence and examining the relevant statutory ingredients, was premature. To the extent that the impugned order may be construed as resulting in the acquittal of the respondents, it is equally unsustainable, as no charge was framed and no evidence was recorded.

22. It is also pertinent to observe that the complaint was instituted on 15.05.2025 and the impugned order was passed on 13.0I.2026, without commencement of trial. Section 5(2) of the Act requires the trial court, after taking cognizance, to proceed with the trial from day to day and conclude it within sixty days, recording sufficient reasons for any delay. The statutory requirement is intended to prevent prolonged uncertainty in disputes involving alleged illegal dispossession and to ensure effective adjudication without compromising the rights of either party. In Rala Khan a. Sohall Arlf Sha,h and, anotler IPLD 2026 SC 4721. tt,.e Hon'ble Supreme Court emphasised that delay in proceedings under the Act undermines the right to fair trial guaranteed by Article 10-A of the Constitution and the policy embodied in Article 37(d) thereof. The directions issued by the Hon'ble Supreme Court require the trial court to maintain a day-to-day order sheet and record specific reasons for delay; avoid routine adjournments; ensure the presence of witnesses and attendance of learned counsel on each date of hearing; and continue the trial notwithstanding a challenge to an interim order before a higher forum, unless a restraining order has been issued by that forum. These requirements must be observed in letter and spirit so that proceedings under the accordance with law.

Act are concluded expeditiously and in 23. For the foregoing reasons, the instant appeal is allowed. The impugned order dated L3.O1.2O26, passed by the learned Additional Sessions Judge-II, Lakki Marwat, in Criminal Complaint No. 4/Comp of 2025, is set aside, and tJle complaint is remanded to the learned trial court for fresh decision on merits, subject to the following directions: (i) The learned trial court shall proceed with the complaint afresh, strictly in accordance with the Act and the law, after affording both parties a lair opportunity of hearing and producing evidence. The complaint shall not be dismissed merely on the ground that a civil suit concerning the same property is pending, unless the learned trial court records a reasoned frnding that the complaint constitutes an abuse ofthe process of law.

(ii) The learned trial court shall conduct the proceedings on a dayto-day basis and endeavour to conclude the trial within sixty days from the date of receipt of a copy of this judgment, in accordance with Section 5(2) of the Act and the directions issued in Raja Khan (supra). In the event that the trial cannot be concluded w.ithin the stipulated period, specific and sufficient reasons shall be recorded in the order sheet, and adjoumments shall not be granted as a matter of routine.

(iii) The complainant shall ensure the presence of his witnesses on every date fixed, while both parties and their learned counsel shall cooperate with the learned trial court 'and attend the proceedings on each date of hearing. Any failure in this regard shall be dealt with in accordance with law.

(iv) The pendency of the civil suit shall neither obstruct nor delay the criminal proceedings. The learned trial court shall decide the complaint independently on the basis of the evidence produced before it, while the civil court shall independently adjudicate upon the civil suit in accordance with law.
